figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1 | Examples of secondary metabolites produced by fungi.  The clinically used antibiotic penicillin is produced 
by Penicillium chrysogenum7. Other clinically used secondary metabolites include immunosuppressants such as the 
cyclosporines and the cholesterol-reducing compound lovastatin, produced by Tolypocladium inflatum and Aspergillus 
terreus, respectively8. Many secondary metabolites have adverse toxic activities, such as the aflatoxins produced by 
Aspergillus flavus and gliotoxin, produced by Aspergillus fumigatus. The toxicity of gliotoxin has been attributed to a 
disulphide bridge that is the functional motif of this metabolite9,117. Aspyridones, from Aspergillus nidulans, have moderate 
cytotoxic activity10. Gibberellins are plant hormones that are also produced by fungi such as Fusarium fujikuroi11. Ergot 
alkaloids are produced by several fungi, including (most prominently) Claviceps purpurea, which produces ergotamines19. 
Light grey indicates non-ribosomal peptide derivatives; dark grey represents a non-ribosomal peptide derivative that 
requires a tryptophan dimethylallyltransferase for synthesis; red represents polyketide derivatives; blue represents a 
mixed polyketide–non-ribosomal peptide compound; green represents a gibberellin, for which synthesis involves terpene 
cyclase but no non-ribosomal peptide synthetase or polyketide synthase.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2 | Gene clusters and enzymes for fungal secondary metabolism.  Gene clusters with a central non-ribosomal 
peptide synthetase (NRPS) gene (left) and polyketide synthase (PKS) gene (right). The domains of the encoded enzymes 
are indicated as spheres, with the minimal domains required to form a module of the enzyme shown in red. These 
enzymes are flanked by a starter ACP transacylase (SAT) domain and a termination domain. The acyltransferase (AT) domain 
selects extender units to add to the product and transfers them to the acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, which loads the 
units to extend the product. Several types of modification can take place on each product intermediate, as indicated by 
the various domains that can be present in the enzyme or encoded by other genes in the cluster: an adenylation (A) domain; 
a condensation (C) domain, which catalyses peptide bond formation; a dehydratase (DH) domain; an epimerization (E) 
domain; an enoyl reductase (ER) domain; a β‑ketoacyl reductase (KR) domain; a ketoacyl synthase (KS) domain, for 
decarboxylative condensation of the extender unit (usually malonyl-CoA or methylmalonyl-CoA) with an acyl thioester; 
a methyltransferase (MT) domain; a peptidyl carrier protein (PCP) domain (also known as thiolation domain), which binds 
the cofactor 4′-phosphopantetheine (4′PP), to which the activated amino acid is covalently attached; a 4′PP transferase 
(PPT) domain, which is typically encoded by another gene in the cluster; and a thioesterase (TE) domain6,16,18,22,23.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3 | Global regulatory proteins involved in the regulation of secondary metabolism gene clusters in various 
fungi.  Environmental signals can influence the regulation of various secondary metabolism gene clusters through 
regulatory proteins that respond to these environmental stimuli and, in turn, modulate the expression of the clusters. 
Shown is a model secondary metabolism gene cluster containing a gene encoding a central non-ribosomal peptide 
synthetase (NRPS), a polyketide synthase (PKS) or a hybrid PKS–NRPS enzyme. CBC, CCAAT-binding complex; CpcR1, 
cephalosporin C regulator 1; LaeA, loss of aflR expression A; RsmA, restorer of secondary metabolism A; SAGA–ADA, 
Spt–Ada–Gcn5–acetyltransferase–ADA.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4 | Pathway-specific regulatory genes and proteins, and crosstalk between 
secondary metabolism gene clusters. Secondary metabolism gene clusters encode 
polyketide synthase (PKS), non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) or hybrid PKS–
NRPS enzymes. Many of these clusters also contain genes encoding transcription factors 
(TFs) that are required for expression of the cluster genes. Dashed arrows indicate 
possible activation by these TFs, in addition to the required activation of PKS/NRPS 
genes. Moreover, crosstalk between clusters has been reported34. In this illustrative 
example, a pathway-specific tf1 gene on chromosome A encodes a TF that activates not 
only its own cluster, but also the pathway-specific tf2 gene of another gene cluster on a 
different chromosome, leading to activation of this second gene cluster.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5 | Chromatin-based regulation of secondary metabolism genes.  Various 
proteins and protein complexes are involved in the regulation of gene clusters through 
chromatin modification; some of these factors mediate the modifications, whereas 
others inhibit such alterations. a | Common histone modifications that are known to be 
involved in secondary metabolism gene regulation include methylation (mono-, di- and 
trimethylation) of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me) and trimethylation of H3 lysine 9 
(H3K9me3). b | Other modifications that are associated with expression from secondary 
metabolism gene clusters include acetylation of H3 lysine 9 and/or H3 lysine 14 (H3K9/
K14ac). HdaA, histone deacetylase A; HepA, heterochromatin protein 1; LaeA, loss of aflR 
expression A; SAGA–ADA, Spt–Ada–Gcn5–acetyltransferase–ADA.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6 | Novel strategies to discover new secondary metabolites.  There are a number of approaches that have been 
used successfully to identify new secondary metabolites that are produced by the polyketide synthase (PKS), non-ribosomal 
peptide synthetase (NRPS) or PKS–NRPS hybrid enzymes encoded by secondary metabolism gene clusters (denoted PKS/
NRPS)6. a | Overexpression of a cluster-specific transcription factor (TF) gene. b | Exchange of promoters for biosynthesis 
genes or TF genes with inducible promoters such as the alcohol dehydrogenase A gene promoter (PalcA). c | Overexpression 
or deletion of a global regulator gene (GR). d | Modification of chromatin. e | Simulation of the physiological or ecological 
conditions that lead to activation of silent gene clusters.
